clue.text: Pay off a humble abode

parts.note: a bung is slang for a bribe, a payment to buy someone off
humble means lowly, low in status

explanation.surface: Someone bribes their way into a modest little home.
explanation.definitionFit: A single-storey house is a kind of dwelling, so an example of an abode.

clue.text: Spy person taking on M's successor

indicators.note: taking on means the person word takes in and holds the next letter

parts.note: bod is informal British slang for a person
the letter following M in the alphabet is N

explanation.surface: A spy is recruited to serve under the new head of the service, M.
explanation.walkthrough: M is also James Bond's boss in the films, which pulls the solver toward MI6 rather than the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional secret agent 007 is the best-known example of a spy.

clue.text: Close second cheated, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: S is a standard abbreviation for second; tricked means deceived or cheated

explanation.surface: A runner-up who finished a close second claims to have been cheated.
explanation.definitionFit: Close in the sense of rigorous or exact, as in close confinement or close attention, is a synonym.

clue.text: Nice touch of Gold Label isn't half cut

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a name is a label or tag

indicators.note: half cut means the word isn't loses its first half, keeping only its back two letters

explanation.surface: A drinker praises a whisky's gold label, implying they are not 'half-cut' (British slang for tipsy).
explanation.definitionFit: A decoration is an added embellishment, a nice finishing touch to something.

clue.text: Turning against one, getting wind up

indicators.note: turning tells us the letters of against one are spun into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone turning against another person, getting the wind up, i.e. becoming scared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting wind up' suggests fear, but 'wind up' here is the British slang for annoying someone deliberately; 'getting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind someone up is British slang for to annoy or provoke them deliberately, so a synonym.

clue.text: Soprano is cold-blooded for the audience

indicators.note: for the audience says the word is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: callous means heartless or cold-blooded

explanation.surface: A critic complains a soprano sings without feeling for her listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Callas was a celebrated Greek-American opera singer, an example of a soprano.

clue.text: Train routes are endlessly reorganised

indicators.note: reorganised says the letters are rearranged into a new order
endlessly means the word are loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A rail company announces its train routes have been reshuffled once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts ARE to AR, which joins ROUTES in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-Channel high-speed rail service is a named example of a train.

clue.text: Beginning to perform in broadcast encore

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the broadcast word

parts.note: to relay a programme is to broadcast or transmit it

indicators.note: beginning to means only the opening letter of perform is used

explanation.surface: A singer starts performing an encore on live television.
explanation.definitionFit: An encore is a repeat performance, which is what a replay gives.

clue.text: Catwalk streak interrupted by posh northern women

indicators.note: interrupted by means the streak word is split open by the other letters

parts.note: a ray is a beam or streak of light
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors

explanation.surface: A streaker runs across a fashion catwalk, disrupting a show of well-to-do northern women.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised platform models walk along is called a runway as well as a catwalk: synonyms.

clue.text: Old French artist practically flipped

indicators.note: flipped says the shortened name is turned back to front
practically means almost all, so the artist's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Edgar Degas was a French Impressionist painter

explanation.surface: An elderly French painter has almost lost his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'practically' trims DEGAS to DEGA, and 'flipped' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged and old are synonyms describing someone advanced in years.

clue.text: Rogue Hollywood guy is relentless

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous rascal or rogue
Hollywood is in Los Angeles, abbreviated LA
a guy is a rope or wire stay, so a cable

explanation.surface: A villainous film-world character who just won't let up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hollywood guy' looks like one film star, but splits into the city and a guy rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cannot be appeased is unyielding, so the word is a synonym of relentless.

clue.text: Bordeaux can't lose at rugby, eliminating Toulouse initially

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of each of the six words before it

explanation.surface: Bordeaux's rugby side is unbeatable, knocking out rivals Toulouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toulouse initially' looks like a single T to remove, but 'initially' covers every word from can't to Toulouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret is the British name for red wine from the Bordeaux region, so Bordeaux defines it by example.

clue.text: Taught again to accept school's head being aloof

indicators.note: to accept means the taught-again word takes the letter in

parts.note: retrained means taught again

indicators.note: head means the first letter of school's

explanation.surface: A teacher is retrained so as to accept the head's rules, becoming distant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reserved and undemonstrative holds back, much as an aloof person does: near synonyms.

clue.text: Boozer in a hole, drunk before work

indicators.note: drunk tells us to stagger the letters of a hole into a new order

parts.note: to use something is to work or operate it

explanation.surface: A man drinking in a dingy dive bar before heading off to his job.
explanation.definitionFit: Boozer is British slang for a pub, and an old-fashioned tavern selling beer is the same thing.

clue.text: Most sage in Kew is established

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: The wisest gardener works at Kew, the famous botanical gardens in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage means wise, so most sage is the superlative of wise.

clue.text: Feeling excited? That is not heartless

parts.note: sent is slang for thrilled or excited, as in music that sends you
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter of not is removed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you are feeling thrilled, and answers that this is not heartless.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentient being is capable of feeling and perceiving, so the adjective matches feeling.

clue.text: Voyage on board takes off

indicators.note: on board means aboard a ship, so the trip goes inside the ship letters

parts.note: board stands for a ship, abbreviated SS for steamship
a trip is a voyage or outing

explanation.surface: A sea voyage gets under way once everyone is on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' is a crossword convention for inside SS, the steamship abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip is to take off one's clothes, so the verb matches takes off.

clue.text: Ushering English Queen into do

indicators.note: into means the English and Queen letters go inside the swindle word

parts.note: a do is a swindle or con, and so is a sting
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: An usher shows an English queen into a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party but is a swindle, STING.
explanation.definitionFit: To usher someone is to guide or direct them, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Plant taken by taste, oddly, for fly

indicators.note: taken by means the plant word is held inside the odd letters
oddly means take the first, third and fifth letters of taste

parts.note: to set seeds is to plant them

explanation.surface: A carnivorous plant catches a fly, lured by its odd taste.
explanation.definitionFit: The African biting insect that carries sleeping sickness is an example of a fly.

clue.text: Following hostilities, blusters for sanctions

indicators.note: following means the bluster word comes after the hostilities word

parts.note: war means hostilities
to rant is to bluster loudly

explanation.surface: After a war, politicians bluster about imposing sanctions.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanction an action is to authorise it, which is what warrants does: synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: Passionate artist's over depression

indicators.note: over says the artist's letters are turned round

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist; the 's is just 'is'
a dent is a hollow or depression

explanation.surface: A passionate painter has got over a period of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' looks like recovery from the depression, but reverses RA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardent means fervent or enthusiastic, so a synonym of passionate.

clue.text: Three quarters welcoming united nation

indicators.note: welcoming means the compass letters surround the united word

parts.note: the quarters are compass points; here south, east and north
to wed is to unite in marriage

explanation.surface: Three regions of a country welcome a unified state.
explanation.walkthrough: Which three compass points must be guessed; WED itself contains W and E, adding to the confusion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scandinavian kingdom is an example of a nation.

clue.text: Dishes out some appetiser vessels

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A waiter hands out starters in little bowls.
explanation.definitionFit: To serve food is to dish it out, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Conduct dire matins when drunk

indicators.note: when drunk tells us to stagger the letters of dire matins into a new order

explanation.surface: A clergyman leads a terrible morning service while intoxicated.
explanation.definitionFit: To administer something is to manage or conduct it, as in administering a ceremony.

clue.text: Marseille, perhaps too French in retrospect

indicators.note: in retrospect means looking back, so the French word is read backwards

parts.note: trop is French for too

explanation.surface: Looking back, Marseille was perhaps too French for a visitor.
explanation.definitionFit: Marseille is a major Mediterranean harbour city, so an example of the general term; perhaps flags the example.

clue.text: Call sweetheart after rift, upset

indicators.note: after puts the sweetheart letter behind the reversed rift
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the rift word is read upwards

parts.note: a gap is a rift or opening
the heart of sweet is its middle letter, E

explanation.surface: After a quarrel, someone is distressed and phones their sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to call them, especially over a public address system.

clue.text: Jail, or bird, ends with isolation ahead

indicators.note: ahead puts the isolation letters in front of the bird
ends means only the first and last letters of isolation

parts.note: a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A prisoner doing 'bird' (British slang for jail time) ends up in solitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird' tempts as prison slang, but here it is the seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern someone is to confine or imprison them, especially in wartime, so a verb synonym of jail.

clue.text: Excitedly greet men coming out

indicators.note: excitedly tells us to agitate the letters of greet men into a new order

explanation.surface: People excitedly greet men as they come out of somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergent describes something emerging or appearing, which is coming out.
